slides.subtitle: The MacBook notch, rebuilt as an on-device AI runtime
body: Native Swift · AppKit + SwiftUI · macOS 15+ · Apple silicon
Technical briefing for developers and partners · October 2026
sparkv.si
slides.notes: SparkV turns the MacBook notch into a control surface: hover the notch and a drawer slides out with media, a file tray, your day, converters, knowledge Spaces and a hub of more than twenty agents. This talk is about how it's built: the window, the activity engine, the on-device AI stack, the privacy model, the developer agents and how we build and ship. Every picture you'll see is a real render from the current source code, not a mock-up. Where something still needs a live check, I'll say so.

slides.subtitle: How a non-activating NSPanel becomes a command center
body: NotchPanel: borderless, non-activating, .statusBar level, on every Space

NotchWindowController owns the controllers and one shared ActivityCenter
Features live in Sources/Labs/<Feature>/ with DESIGN.md and INTEGRATION.md

slides.notes: The whole app is one borderless, non-activating panel at status-bar level. It joins every Space, including full-screen apps, never steals focus, and lets clicks fall through while the island is closed. AppKit normally pushes windows below the menu bar, so the panel overrides constrainFrameRect to sit at the absolute top edge. The window controller owns 31 long-lived feature objects plus the shared ActivityCenter. New features are built in isolation in a Labs folder: a DESIGN.md with the research and decisions, an INTEGRATION.md with exact wiring steps, then one copy line in build.sh. Only the lead touches the four shared files, which is what let us build features in parallel without merge fights.

slides.header: Live activities with Dynamic Island rules
slides.subtitle: A priority queue that never covers your work
body: Compact wings grow sideways inside the menu bar, 30–112 pt per side
Alerts of 8 s or less queue by priority; time runs only on screen
Preempted alerts resume; anything waiting 12 s is dropped
Persistent activities peek for 4 s, then rest in the wings
slides.status: Bands render from source; key interception, banners and Bluetooth need a live check.
slides.notes: The closed island follows Dynamic Island rules. Compact activities grow sideways inside the menu-bar height, so nothing below the menu bar is covered. Short alerts go into a priority queue whose clock only runs while they're visible, so a notification can't eat the charging alert. Volume and brightness are live feedback: newest wins and they're never replayed. Long-running things like a timer, a meeting or a recording peek in the band for four seconds and then tuck into the wings. All of this is one ActivityCenter, and every feature posts a LiveActivity with a priority, an optional compact form and a tab to open on hover. Honest status: the bands render from source, but key interception, banners and AirPods need the running app to confirm.

slides.subtitle: Apple frameworks first; the network is opt-in

Vision · OCR everywhere, face landmarks for Screen Distance

Translation · TranslationSession cached per language pair
ScreenCaptureKit · stills for Ask Screen, SCStream audio for meetings

tiles.label: dictation cleanup, summaries, replies, prompts, plans
OCR everywhere, face landmarks for Screen Distance
stills for Ask Screen, SCStream audio for meetings
language ID and entities for Spaces

slides.notes: Ten files use the on-device Apple Intelligence model through FoundationModels: Tray AI, Clicky, dictation formatting, meeting summaries and answers, Reply Drafter, Prompt Refiner, Live Translation's fallback, Ask Screen, Flow Canvas and Downloads. One constraint shaped the code: we build with the Command Line Tools only, and the @Generable macro plugin isn't part of them, so guided generation uses DynamicGenerationSchema built at runtime. The model has a 4096-token context, so meeting transcripts are chunked. Speech uses the new SpeechAnalyzer and SpeechTranscriber on macOS 26 and falls back to SFSpeechRecognizer. ScreenCaptureKit gives us stills with SparkV's own windows excluded, and an SCStream with capturesAudio for meeting audio, which is why no bot has to join a call.

slides.subtitle: Speech in, structured text out, on the Mac
body: Dictation: hold fn → on-device transcript → cleanup → typed at the cursor
Meetings: mic plus system audio, no bot joins, guided JSON summaries
Translation order: Apple Translation → on-device model → Groq if allowed
Warm translation: 0.33–0.8 s per caption
slides.status: Audio capture and the fn key need a live check; views render from saved data.
slides.notes: Three pipelines share one pattern: capture on device, recognise on device, structure with the on-device model. Dictation formats text with a prewarmed LanguageModelSession so the cleanup is fast when you release fn. Meetings record your mic and the meeting's audio through ScreenCaptureKit, transcribe on device and produce minutes, decisions and your tasks as guided JSON. Live Translation tries Apple Translation first, falls back to the on-device model when a language pair isn't downloaded, and uses Groq only if the user turned on that specific toggle. Cold sessions take two to three seconds; warm ones under a second per caption, which is why sessions are cached per pair.

slides.subtitle: Nothing leaves the Mac unless the user brings a key
body: On device: speech, camera, screenshots, clipboard, Spaces, meeting audio
Groq: per-feature toggle, off by default, the buyer's own key
While a toggle is off, the keychain is never read
Clipboard history starts off; concealed and transient copies are skipped
12 permissions, each asked only when the user clicks Allow
slides.notes: The privacy model is simple to state and easy to audit. Speech, camera, screen captures, clipboard, Spaces and meeting audio stay on the Mac. Groq is the only cloud path, and it's opt-in per feature: Clicky, Tray AI, meetings, Live Translation, Flow Canvas and UI Audit summaries each have their own switch, default off, using the buyer's own key. When a switch is off the code doesn't even read the keychain item. Clipboard history is off until you turn it on, and it honours the pasteboard conventions password managers use to mark concealed or transient copies. Setup asks for nothing up front: each of the 12 permissions is requested only when you click Allow, and every feature works in a reduced way without it. License checks, when they ship, will send the key, an anonymous device ID and the app version to Lemon Squeezy, and nothing else. There are no analytics.

slides.header: UI Audit: a QA agent for your own site
slides.subtitle: Playwright and axe-core, started from the notch
body: Swift spawns node audit.mjs: JSON lines out; pause, resume, stop in
Crawl, forms, axe-core WCAG 2.2 AA, 1440/390 px layout, Tab order
Origin allow-list; writes blocked off test hosts; risky clicks skipped
P copies a fix prompt for Claude Code, Cursor or Copilot
slides.notes: UI Audit audits websites you own. The Swift controller writes a run config, starts a Node runner with Playwright and axe-core, and talks to it over JSON lines: plan, page, step and finding events come out; pause, resume and stop go in. If the app dies, stdin closes and the runner stops, so you never leak a crawler. The runner crawls, checks layout at 1440 and 390 pixels, walks the Tab order, runs axe-core for WCAG 2.2 A and AA, and fills forms with type-correct test data. The safety model is strict: navigation outside the allowed origins is aborted, every non-GET request is blocked unless the host is local or test or you opt in for this run, and anything that looks like pay, delete or log out is never clicked. The numbers are from a real end-to-end run against our planted-issue test site: 69 findings, an on-device summary, and a 51,666-character fix prompt. The runner's own self-test passes 48 of 48, including the checks that it never hit the logout or delete URLs. It needs Node 20 and Playwright's Chromium on the machine today.

slides.header: Browser Flows: record once, replay with data
slides.subtitle: Self-healing selectors; secrets are never stored
body: Each step stores ranked selectors and an element fingerprint
Healing accepts a match of 0.6 or more that clearly beats the runner-up
Passwords become {{password}}, asked at replay, sent over stdin
CSV loop: one replay per row, up to 500 rows
slides.status: Self-test not yet clean under load: one replay timed out, one CSV loop hung. Fix before launch.
slides.notes: Browser Flows records a browser task once and replays it. Each recorded step keeps an ordered list of selectors, in the spirit of Selenium IDE's targets list, plus a fingerprint of the element: tag, role, accessible name, text, attributes and ancestor path. When every selector fails, the runner scores all elements against the fingerprint and accepts the best one only if it scores at least 0.6 and clearly beats the runner-up, then writes the healed selector first. Password, card, CVV, OTP and SSN fields are never read: they become variables and are passed over stdin at replay, never on the command line. Flows that mention purchase, payment or delete need an explicit confirmation. Honest status: the recorder self-test isn't clean yet; under heavy load one replay timed out and a CSV loop hung. That's on the roadmap before launch.

slides.header: Flow Canvas: workflows as a graph
slides.subtitle: Sources in, actions chained, run on this Mac
body: Drop links, PDFs, screenshots and notes as source cards
Chain extract, compare, summarize, report and chat-with-sources
"Suggest steps" plans the chain from one sentence
Export to Markdown, PDF, CSV, Tray, Notes or a Space
slides.notes: Flow Canvas is a whiteboard for AI workflows. Source cards hold links, PDFs, screenshots or notes; action cards extract fields, compare, summarize or write a report; edges carry data between them, and Run all executes the graph. You can also describe the goal in one sentence and Suggest steps builds the chain. It ships with four templates, including the competitor pricing comparison you see here. The engine indicator top right says 'On this Mac': FoundationModels, Vision OCR and Apple Translation do the work. Groq is a separate opt-in for this feature only. Canvases are plain versioned JSON in Application Support, and dropped files are copied into the canvas's assets folder; originals are never moved.

slides.subtitle: A small toolchain and strict habits
body: CLT-only · one zsh build script, no Xcode project required
No macro plugins · no @State, #Preview, @Entry, @Generable
Temp-dir builds · iCloud can't modify files mid-compile
Stable signing · permission grants survive every rebuild
Hardened Runtime · explicit camera, mic, calendar, Apple Events entitlements
Real-source harnesses · Swift 5 and 6, private pasteboards

tiles.label: one zsh build script, no Xcode project required
explicit camera, mic, calendar, Apple Events entitlements

slides.notes: We build with the Command Line Tools only. build.sh copies sources into a temp folder, compiles GlanceKit as a static library with its own concurrency settings, compiles the app, builds the Now Playing adapter framework with clang, signs nested code first and then the app with the Hardened Runtime. The temp folder exists because the project lives on iCloud Desktop, which touches files mid-build and adds Finder attributes codesign rejects. No Xcode means no macro plugins, so the code avoids @State, #Preview, @Entry and @Generable. A stable self-signed identity, 'NotchIsland Developer', gives every build the same designated requirement, so Accessibility and Screen Recording grants survive rebuilds. Tests are harnesses that compile the real app sources, for example the clipboard harness runs against private named pasteboards, never the general one, in both Swift 5 and Swift 6 modes. The log scale is there because the widget harness sweeps time zones and has far more checks than the others; don't read it as a coverage ranking.

body: Why not the App Store: Accessibility, event taps, private frameworks, child processes
Developer ID pipeline: cert, sign with timestamp, notarize, staple, Sparkle 2, License API
slides.notes: SparkV can't be sandboxed. Apple's DTS says Accessibility APIs aren't compatible with the App Sandbox, and we also need event taps for the fn key, posted key events for paste, private DisplayServices for the HUD, the MediaRemote adapter for Now Playing, and child processes for Node and Shortcuts. NotchNook stays off the App Store for the same MediaRemote reason. So we ship direct: a Developer ID certificate replaces today's local identity, every nested binary is signed with the Hardened Runtime and a secure timestamp, the DMG is notarized and stapled, and Sparkle 2 delivers updates from a signed appcast. Since Sequoia, an un-notarized app can't be opened with right-click Open, so notarization isn't optional for a paid product. The local identity stays for development builds. Sources for the sandbox constraints are in the business plan, section 5.

slides.notes: The launch plan is thirty days. The engineering-heavy parts are days 8 to 15: licensing with Lemon Squeezy's License API, Keychain-stored trial dates, a 14-day offline grace window, gating at the window controller so locked features never even instantiate, Sparkle, and a notarized DMG, then a clean-Mac test on a fresh user account. Two known blockers are explicit: Face Unlock comes out of the commercial build because of the ArcFace licence, and UI Audit and Browser Flows currently need Node on the buyer's Mac. After 1.0 the first engineering item is making the Browser Flows self-test pass reliably. Shared Spaces today is a file package; live sync doesn't exist and we don't advertise it.
